```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(distsamp)
```

## What this package does

A density surface model needs survey effort cut into short pieces of roughly
equal length, called *segments*. Each segment has a location, an amount of
effort, and a count of what was seen along it. `distsamp` builds that segment
table from line-transect data in the format of the North Atlantic Right Whale
Consortium (NARWC) sightings database.

The input format is defined in Kenney (2023), *The North Atlantic Right Whale
Consortium Database: A Guide for Users and Contributors*, Version 8 (the
"handbook"). The output can be passed to `Distance` or `dsm`.

## Read the data

`read_narwc()` standardises column names and types. It accepts the handbook's
`LAT_DD`/`LONG_DD` and the `LATITUDE`/`LONGITUDE` spelling used in extracts
from the database manager.

```{r}
path <- system.file("extdata", "narwc-example.csv", package = "distsamp")
dat <- read_narwc(path)

dim(dat)
head(dat[, c("FILEID", "EVENTNO", "TIME", "LATITUDE", "LEGTYPE", "LEGSTAGE", "SPECCODE")])
```

**All data in this vignette is synthetic.** `narwc-example.csv` is a two-day
survey generated by `data-raw/make-fixture.R`. It mirrors the hypothetical
survey in Figure 2 of the handbook: transits, survey lines, sightings sharing
an event number, a pilot sighting, a cross-leg, a break-off to circle, and a
line abandoned and re-flown later the same day. Positions, dates, and animals
are invented. Every line runs due north along one meridian in 0.01-degree
steps, so expected distances can be checked by hand.

No real NARWC records are distributed with the package or were used to develop
it. The numbers here show the mechanics only; none is a result. Real data must
be requested from the [NARWC](https://www.narwc.org/sightings-database.html).
Validation against a real extract is still an open item.

## Handle columns a survey programme adds

Survey programmes add their own derived columns. `read_narwc()` keeps the
handbook columns, drops the rest, and reports what it dropped:

```{r}
ccs <- read.csv(path)
ccs$Tr_SIGHTING <- 1
ccs$IS_LAT <- ccs$LAT_DD
ccs$IS_LONG <- ccs$LONG_DD

kept <- read_narwc(ccs)
```

`narwc_profiles()` lists what is known about each programme's columns, with a
confidence level:

```{r}
narwc_profiles("ccs")[, c("column", "role", "confidence")]
```

Naming the profile keeps them:

```{r}
names(read_narwc(ccs, profile = "ccs"))[10:14]
```

Keeping a column is not interpreting it. A profile is never applied because a
column name matched, and `distsamp` only carries these columns. In a CCS file
`Tr_SIGHTING` means "sighting made from the track-line", but another programme
could use the same name for something else. A column name is not a contract
between programmes.

## Fill values recorded only when they change

NARWC often records a value once and leaves it blank until it changes. For
example, `LEGTYPE` is entered at the start of a census line and left empty
below. `fill_narwc()` carries that state forward:

```{r}
gappy <- data.frame(
  FILEID = "A", DATE = as.Date("2024-04-01"), EVENTNO = 1:6,
  LEGTYPE  = c(2, NA, NA, NA, 1, NA),
  BEAUFORT = c(2, NA, NA, 4, NA, NA)
)
fill_narwc(gappy)
```

It differs from a bare `tidyr::fill()` in three ways.

**It groups by file and day.** Without grouping, the sea state from the last
record of one day carries into the next, and a leg number crosses into another
survey. A filled value cannot be told apart from a recorded one afterwards, so
the error cannot be found later.

**It refuses to fill sighting columns.** Carrying `SPECCODE` and `NUMBER`
forward would copy one group of three right whales onto every row until the
next sighting:

```{r, error = TRUE}
fill_narwc(gappy, columns = "NUMBER")
```

**It reports recovered and inferred values separately.** `"downup"` fills down,
then up. The upward fills are values before the first record of a group, which
were never logged. Only the downward fills recover recorded state, so the
report counts the two apart.

Filling `LEGSTAGE` is the least safe default. If a file records `1` (begin
line) and leaves the continuation rows blank, filling down marks the whole line
`1` instead of `2` (continue). On-effort eligibility is `LEGSTAGE == 2`, so
that line drops out of every distance calculation. Check the per-column counts
against what you expect.

## Check the data

`validate_narwc()` reports problems without raising errors or modifying the
data.

```{r}
validate_narwc(dat)
```

The fixture gives one note. A survey line was abandoned when the sea state
rose, so it has no end-line record. Lines abandoned or re-flown later
legitimately lack one, so this is a note, not a warning. On a line flown to
completion, a missing end-line means the record is incomplete.

Real data typically also gives codes outside the handbook's code book,
sightings recorded at line-boundary events, `LEGSTAGE` sequences that do not
close, and gaps in required fields. Each finding names the rows involved:

```{r}
broken <- dat
broken$LEGTYPE[1] <- 8       # not a NARWC LEGTYPE
broken$LONGITUDE <- abs(broken$LONGITUDE)  # sign convention lost

issues <- validate_narwc(broken)
issues[, c("check", "severity", "column", "n")]
issues$message[1]
```

## Segment the survey

`segment_survey()` runs the whole pipeline.

```{r}
segs <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1)
segs
```

The `segments` table has one row per segment:

```{r}
head(segs$segments[, c("seg_id", "LEGNO3", "seg_eff", "mid_lat", "mid_lon", "wt_beaufort")])
```

- `seg_eff`: the segment's realised length, in km.
- `mid_lat`/`mid_lon`: the point halfway along the segment's effort. Use it
  for covariate lookups.
- `wt_beaufort`: mean sea state, weighted by the distance each record covers.
  This is the form to use as a detection covariate.

Counts are in a separate table, one row per segment per species:

```{r}
head(segs$sightings)
```

For a density surface model, spread them across columns:

```{r}
wide <- segments_wide(segs)
head(wide[, c("seg_id", "seg_eff", "mid_lat", "mid_lon", "n_RIWH", "n_FIWH")])
```

### Effort is conserved

Every kilometre of on-effort trackline is in exactly one segment.

```{r}
sum(segs$tracks$track_effort)
sum(segs$segments$seg_eff)
```

### Reproducibility

Segmentation makes two random choices: which segment absorbs a track's
leftover distance, and whether a segment that cannot match its target exactly
runs long or short. With a `seed`, a run repeats exactly.

```{r}
a <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1)
b <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1)
identical(a$segments, b$segments)

c <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 2)
identical(a$segments$seg_eff, c$segments$seg_eff)
```

The session's own random stream is not changed.

## Choose a distance method

```{r}
dist_methods()
```

Becker's `segchopr` routine and Kenney and Winn (1986) use the same formula:
the spherical law of cosines, scaled by 111.12 km per degree. The choice
between them does not change results:

```{r}
gc_distance(43, -69, 44, -70, method = "becker") ==
  gc_distance(43, -69, 44, -70, method = "kenney")
```

Both names are kept so existing scripts read sensibly and so you can record
which lineage you followed. The default, `"haversine"`, uses the same sphere
but stays numerically stable at the short ranges between consecutive records,
where the law of cosines loses precision.

```{r}
segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1, dist_method = "becker")$settings$dist_method
```

## Define effort

`flag_effort()` decides which records are on effort. The defaults follow the
CETAP standard: on a survey line (`LEGTYPE == 2`), Beaufort 3 or less, below
1,200 ft, and visibility of at least 2 nautical miles.

```{r}
table(flag_effort(dat)$OnOff.Effort)
table(flag_effort(dat, max_beaufort = 1)$OnOff.Effort)
```

`VISIBLTY` holds two encodings in one column. Since 2004 it is a distance in
nautical miles. Before that it held a code, stored as a negative number. `-1`
means *clear for at least 2 nautical miles*, which is good conditions, so a
plain `VISIBLTY >= 2` test discards every legacy record.

```{r}
visibility_ok(c(5, 1.5, -1, -2))
```

## Define sightings

Only detections made during standard search effort belong in a density
estimate. By default the package excludes:

- sightings by anyone other than an on-duty observer (`LEGSTAGE == 6`);
- sightings found afterwards in a vertical photograph (`LEGSTAGE == 7`);
- identifications that are only possible or unrecorded (`IDREL` of 1 or 9).

```{r}
strict <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1)
loose <- segment_survey(
  dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1,
  sighting_args = list(legstage_exclude = numeric(0), idrel_keep = 1:3)
)

sum(strict$sightings$n_sightings)
sum(loose$sightings$n_sightings)
```

A group sighted from the track and then circled for photographs has its
position recorded off effort. These detections are attached back to the
segment they came from. Following the CETAP rule, only further groups *of the
same species* count with the original:

```{r}
sapply(c("none", "same_species", "all"), function(m) {
  s <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1, circling = m)
  sum(s$sightings$n_animals[s$sightings$SPECCODE == "RIWH"])
})
```

## Perpendicular distances

The *perpendicular distance* is the distance from the track-line to the
animal, measured at right angles to the track. Surveys that record the
`ANGLEL`/`ANGLER` declination angles get perpendicular distances computed
automatically, in a `detections` table shaped for a detection function.

```{r}
head(segs$detections)
```

The geometry is handbook 8.A.2. The angle is measured below the horizon when
the sighting is abeam, so the distance is `ALT / tan(angle)`.

```{r}
# 45 degrees below the horizon at 229 m puts the animal 229 m off the track
perp_distance(45, altitude = 229)
perp_distance(c(75, 60, 45, 30, 15), altitude = 229)
```

Angles replaced `STRIP` in 2022. Survey altitudes rose once offshore wind
turbines were in place. `STRIP`'s fixed distance intervals shift with altitude;
an angle does not.

### Distances before 2022: `STRIP`

Angles exist only from 2022. The archive records right-angle distance in three
other ways, each with its own function.

`STRIP` is an *interval*, not a point, read off calibrated markings on the
observation bubble. Handbook 8.A.31 defines two code books. Which one applies
depends on the programme, the date, and the aircraft, so one code can mean
different things:

```{r}
strip_distance(c(5, 13), scheme = "cetap", units = "nmi")
strip_distance(c(5, 13), scheme = "nlpsc", units = "nmi")
```

Code 13 is 1–2 nmi under CETAP and over 4 nmi under NLPSC. Reading a code with
the wrong book gives plausible but wrong distances, and nothing downstream
detects it. With `scheme = "auto"` the book is chosen from the survey date.
With neither a date nor a scheme, the function errors rather than guess.
`narwc_strip_bins()` prints either book in full.

### Exact sighting positions

Where `S_LAT`/`S_LONG` exist, the perpendicular distance is measured, not
inferred. `exact_distance()` projects the sighting onto the track-line:

```{r}
prepped <- flag_effort(make_leg_id(dat))
ex <- exact_distance(prepped)
subset(cbind(prepped["SPECCODE"], ex), !is.na(distance))
```

`along` is how far the aircraft was from abeam when the sighting was logged.
Measuring straight to the animal instead gives `sqrt(distance^2 + along^2)`.
That radial distance is always too large, which widens the fitted strip and
biases density down. The row with `along` of 300 m has a radial distance more
than twice its perpendicular one.

### Sightings logged while circling

These are usually real on-effort detections: the animal was seen from the
track-line, which is why the aircraft left it. `circling_distance()` ties each
one to the `LEGSTAGE == 3` break-off record and measures from there:

```{r}
circ <- circling_distance(flag_circling(make_leg_id(dat)))
subset(circ, !is.na(distance))
```

`radial` is the straight-line distance from the break-off point. `distance` is
that distance projected onto the census line. This is a weaker source than the
other three, because the position is fixed minutes after detection and the
animal has moved. Exclude these from a detection function unless including
them is a deliberate, stated choice.

### Distance units

`ALT` is in metres, so distances are in metres by default. `seg_eff` is in
kilometres. Passing both to `Distance::ds()` without reconciling them scales
density by 1000. Use `distance_units = "km"`, or supply `convert_units`
(0.001 for distances in m and effort in km).

```{r}
segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1,
               distance_units = "km")$detections$distance[1:3]
```

### Circling detections have no distance

Circled animals still count towards a segment's abundance. A position logged
off the track is not a perpendicular distance, so it must not be fitted. By
default (`circling_distance = "with_group"`) circled animals are added to the
group they were counted with and get no detection row of their own:

```{r}
subset(segs$detections, circling == 1)
```

Distances are restricted to on-effort census records by default. Handbook
8.A.31 notes that some teams record angles during transits and circling for
practice, and those must not enter a detection function.

## Plot the result

Four diagnostic views show what the tables make hard to see. They need
`ggplot2` and return ordinary `ggplot` objects.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(segs)
```

The track flown is pale grey, segment midpoints dark grey, and sightings are
coloured by species. A failed segmentation is usually obvious here: midpoints
along a line the aircraft never flew, or bunched where a track should have
split.

Both layers are capped on purpose. Midpoints shrink as their number grows,
because 19,774 of them at a readable size cover the survey area in solid
black. Only the `max_legend` most-seen species keep their own colour; the rest
are grouped as "other", so a survey with 36 species still has a readable
legend. Nothing is dropped from the map. `species = "RIWH"` pulls any one
species back out.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(segs, what = "tracks")
```

The same positions, coloured by `new_trackno`. This view shows whether track
splitting worked. A break in effort should start a new colour, and one colour
should never span two places the aircraft could not have flown between. Look
at the fixture's re-flown line.

Past `max_legend` tracks, colours repeat and the legend is dropped. A
130-entry legend squeezes the map into a corner, and 130 colours cannot be told
apart. Neighbouring tracks still differ, which is what the view is for.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(segs, what = "effort")
```

Segment lengths against the target, with the tolerance band dashed. Some
spread is expected, because the Becker method gives each track one absorbing
segment that takes the remainder. Many segments outside the band are not
expected.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(segs, what = "distances")
```

The detection-function diagnostic. Look at it before calling `Distance::ds()`.
Expect a shoulder near zero and a tail that falls away.

Two cautions:

- A dip in the first bin need not be a sampling artefact. An aircraft cannot
  see the water directly beneath it, and the handbook says so outright for the
  Skymaster. That is a reason to truncate on the left, not to assume the
  animals were absent.
- A smooth curve is not evidence that `g(0) = 1` (detection on the line is
  certain). Animals submerged when the aircraft passed leave no trace in this
  plot.

The axis stops at the 99th percentile. The subtitle states how many detections
lie beyond it and how large the largest is. On one real archive, a single
distance of six thousand kilometres set the scale and put all 2,170 real
distances in the first bin. A distance that large is a broken record, not a
wide detection, and the subtitle says so. Nothing is removed from the data,
only from the view.

For a map with coastlines, pass the positions to `sf`.

## Plot part of a survey

An archive spanning decades plots as a smear. Every plotting function takes
`dates`, `years`, and `months`. These narrow together: `years = 2019,
months = 8` is August 2019, not all of 2019 plus every August.

```r
plot_survey(air, "occupations", years = 2019, months = 8)
plot(segs, what = "tracks", dates = "2019-08-14")
```

`filter_days()` makes the same selection without plotting. Asking for days the
data does not hold is an error that reports which days the data covers.

## Spatial output

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)}
pts <- segments_as_sf(segs, "midpoints")
lines <- segments_as_sf(segs, "lines")
lines[1:3, c("seg_id", "seg_eff")]
```

Cropping applies to the whole result and keeps the tables consistent:

```{r}
gom <- c(xmin = -69.05, xmax = -68.5, ymin = 42, ymax = 48)
nrow(crop_to_bbox(segs, gom)$segments)
```

## Write results

The package writes nothing to disk unless asked.

```{r}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "segments")
write_segments(segs, out)
list.files(out)
```

## Prepare a real extract

The fixture is clean. A real NARWC extract is not, and the preparation steps
must run in a fixed order. Getting the order wrong raises no error.
`prepare_survey()` runs them:

```{r}
air <- prepare_survey(dat, quiet = TRUE)
c(records = nrow(air), on_effort = sum(air$OnOff.Effort == 1))
```

In order, it builds line occupations, fills line state recorded only at change
points, classifies the platform by speed, keeps that platform's records, and
flags effort. `?prepare_survey` lists which step depends on which. Two examples
of why the order matters:

- Filtering out a vessel leg *before* occupations are built makes two
  occupations of one survey line adjacent. They merge, and the ferry between
  them counts as survey effort. On real data this gave 224.5 km where 4.4 km
  was correct.
- `LEGSTAGE` is recorded when it changes, so most mid-line records carry none,
  and a right-angle distance needs `LEGSTAGE == 2`. On one archive this left
  1,928 of 2,280 on-effort census sightings with no distance.

Then look at the data before trusting any number from it:

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_survey(air, "occupations", coastline = FALSE)
```

A survey line drawn in three pieces, or three lines drawn as one, shows here
and not in a table. `diagnose_pipeline()` gives the same check as numbers. The
problems real extracts cause are listed in
`docs/08-onboarding-a-real-extract.md`.

If a view will not draw because the column it colours by does not exist yet,
use `"positions"`. It needs only `LATITUDE` and `LONGITUDE`, so it works on a
file that has not been prepared, or whose columns are not what was expected.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_survey(air, "positions", sightings = TRUE, coastline = FALSE)
```

With `sightings = TRUE` this shows where the aircraft went and what was seen.
Sightings are taken before thinning and drawn as outlined markers on their own
scale, so they stand out from the effort. Otherwise a few thousand sighting
rows among three million would not survive `max_points`.

## Run the steps yourself

Every stage is exported, so you can intervene between them:

```{r}
step <- dat |>
  make_leg_id() |>          # separate re-occupations of a line
  flag_circling() |>        # mark records taken while circling
  flag_effort() |>          # decide what is on effort
  point_to_point_effort() |># great-circle distance along the track
  split_tracks()            # start a new track where effort breaks

tracks <- track_effort(step)
plan <- plan_segments(tracks, seg_length = 5, seed = 1)
head(plan)
```

## Citation

The segmentation method is Becker et al. (2010); the package is an
implementation of it. Cite both, and record the `seed`. Without it the
segmentation is not reproducible.

The published method states the target segment length and that segments are
cut from continuous effort. It does not say what happens to the leftover
distance at the end of a track. The tolerance test and the random choice of an
absorbing segment come from Becker's `segchopr` code. `?plan_segments` is the
documentation of record for them.
